title: Trade, Tourism and Environmental Issues
syllabus: WAEC Geography, Regional Geography of Nigeria: trade; tourism; development and environmental issues; ECOWAS. Part A: environmental problems and conservation; Part B: trade, tourism
NERDC-based schemes: Commercial activities in Nigeria; Trade; Tourism; Environmental problems; Environmental conservation
objectives: distinguish between internal (domestic) and international trade and describe Nigeria's main exports and imports;
explain the importance of trade and the role of ECOWAS;
identify major tourist attractions and explain the importance and problems of tourism;
describe Nigeria's main environmental problems, their causes and effects;
suggest ways of managing and conserving the environment.
explain the meaning of the balance of trade and calculate it from given figures;
intro: Trade connects Nigeria's producers with markets at home and abroad; tourism turns natural beauty and culture into income; and the environment underpins both. This final lesson in the Nigeria series brings these together, because how Nigeria trades and develops directly affects its environment.

blocks.text: **Trade** is the buying and selling (or exchange) of goods and services. **Internal (domestic) trade** takes place within Nigeria; **international (foreign) trade** takes place between Nigeria and other countries.

items: **Internal trade** happens in daily and periodic markets, shops and, increasingly, online. Large markets such as Onitsha Main Market, Ariaria in Aba, Balogun in Lagos and Dawanau grain market near Kano serve traders from across Nigeria and neighbouring countries. Goods move between regions because each produces different things — for example grains and livestock from the north, and palm produce and manufactured goods from the south.

**Exports**: crude oil dominates. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, crude oil made up about 69% of the value of Nigeria's exports in the last quarter of 2024. Other exports include liquefied natural gas, refined petroleum products, cocoa, sesame seeds, cashew nuts and urea fertiliser.
**Imports** include machinery, vehicles, chemicals, wheat and other foods, and manufactured consumer goods. Nigeria long imported most of its petrol; new domestic refining capacity is changing this.

blocks.text: Trade earns foreign exchange, provides government revenue through taxes and duties, creates jobs and gives people access to goods they cannot produce locally. Dependence on one main export, however, leaves the economy vulnerable when oil prices fall.

The **balance of trade** is the difference between the value of a country's exports and imports of goods. It is **favourable** (a surplus) when exports are worth more than imports, and **unfavourable** (a deficit) when imports are worth more. Because crude oil dominates Nigeria's exports, the balance of trade rises and falls with the world price of oil.

The **Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)** was founded by the Treaty of Lagos in **1975** to promote economic co-operation and integration among West African countries. Its headquarters (the ECOWAS Commission) is in **Abuja**.

items: **Aims and achievements**: free movement of people (ECOWAS citizens can travel within the region without visas), reduction of trade barriers, regional infrastructure such as roads, and peace-keeping and conflict mediation.
**Problems**: poor road and rail links between countries, different currencies, smuggling and illegal checkpoints, political instability, and differences in national policies.
Nigeria is also a member of the wider **African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)**, which aims to increase trade between African countries.

items.title: Importance
items.text: Earns income and foreign exchange, creates jobs (hotels, guides, transport, crafts), encourages conservation of wildlife and heritage, and promotes national unity and cultural pride.

items.title: Problems
items.text: Insecurity in some regions, poor roads and facilities, irregular power and water, weak maintenance of sites, limited publicity and high costs.

blocks.text: Solutions include improving security and infrastructure, training hospitality workers, maintaining and promoting sites, and involving local communities so that they benefit from tourism.

blocks.text: Two recent examples show the scale of these problems. In **2022**, floods affected 33 of Nigeria's 36 states; the federal government reported over 600 deaths and more than 1.4 million people displaced, after unusually heavy rainfall and the release of water from Cameroon's Lagdo Dam. In the north-east, the open-water area of **Lake Chad** has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s — by about 90% according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization — although its size varies from year to year. The main causes are the severe droughts of the 1970s and 1980s and increased use of water for irrigation and other needs.

In the Niger Delta, a 2011 UN Environment Programme assessment of Ogoniland reported widespread oil contamination of land and water; a government clean-up programme (HYPREP) was later set up to address it.

items: **Afforestation and the Great Green Wall** to slow desertification; shelter belts and controlled grazing.
**Erosion control**: planting vegetation, terracing, drainage channels and check dams in gully areas.
**Flood management**: early warning, clearing drains, controlling building on floodplains, better dam coordination and new reservoirs.
**Oil industry regulation**: reducing gas flaring, maintaining pipelines, prompt clean-up of spills and compensation for affected communities.
**Urban waste management**: regular collection, recycling and public education.
**Laws and agencies**: environmental protection laws and agencies, and public awareness through schools and the media.

blocks.text: Environmental figures change over time. Always use the latest reliable source and quote the year of any figure you give in an examination.

worked.title: Calculating a percentage share
worked.problem: In a quarter, a country's total exports were worth ₦20 trillion, of which crude oil was worth ₦13.8 trillion. What percentage of exports was crude oil, and what does this show?
steps: Interpretation: more than two-thirds of export earnings come from one product, so the economy depends heavily on oil and is exposed to changes in oil prices.
worked.note: Figures rounded from NBS data for the fourth quarter of 2024.

worked.title: Calculating a balance of trade
worked.problem: In one year a country's exports were worth ₦18 trillion and its imports ₦15 trillion. Calculate its balance of trade and say whether it is favourable.
steps: Balance of trade = value of exports − value of imports.
Exports are worth more than imports, so the balance is **favourable** (a surplus).

exam_tips: Give named examples for tourist attractions and environmental problems: examiners reward specific places.
For environmental questions, organise your answer as causes, effects and solutions.
Remember ECOWAS facts: founded 1975 by the Treaty of Lagos; headquarters in Abuja.

checks.q: What is the difference between internal and international trade?
checks.a: Internal trade happens within Nigeria; international trade is between Nigeria and other countries.

checks.q: Name Nigeria's two UNESCO World Heritage sites.
checks.a: Sukur Cultural Landscape (1999) and Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (2005).

checks.q: Give one cause and one effect of desertification in northern Nigeria.
checks.a: Cause: overgrazing or low, unreliable rainfall. Effect: loss of farmland and pasture, leading to migration.

checks.q: Name the two UNESCO World Heritage sites in Nigeria and their states.
checks.a: Sukur Cultural Landscape (Adamawa State, inscribed 1999) and Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (Osun State, inscribed 2005).

checks.q: Give two effects of gas flaring in the Niger Delta.
checks.a: It pollutes the air and can harm people's health, and it wastes natural gas that could be used for power or exports. Heat and soot also affect crops and vegetation near flare sites.

summary: Internal trade links regions through large markets; international trade is dominated by crude oil exports, with imports of machinery, vehicles, chemicals and food.
ECOWAS (1975, headquarters Abuja) promotes regional integration but faces infrastructure and policy barriers.
Tourist attractions include Obudu, Yankari, the two UNESCO sites and many festivals; insecurity and poor facilities limit tourism.
Major environmental problems include desertification, gully erosion, flooding, oil pollution, deforestation, coastal erosion and urban waste; each needs specific management measures.

structured.q: (a) Name three tourist attractions in Nigeria and the states where they are found. (b) Explain three problems facing tourism in Nigeria. (c) Suggest two solutions.
model: (a) Obudu Mountain Resort — Cross River; Yankari Game Reserve — Bauchi; Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove — Osun (Olumo Rock — Ogun; Argungu Fishing Festival — Kebbi; Sukur — Adamawa also accepted).

(b) 1. Insecurity discourages visitors. 2. Poor roads, power and water supplies make sites hard to reach and uncomfortable. 3. Poor maintenance and limited publicity reduce the attractiveness and visibility of sites.
(c) Improve security and infrastructure; maintain and promote sites with community involvement.

structured.q: (a) Describe the causes and effects of oil pollution in the Niger Delta. (b) Suggest three ways of reducing it.
model: (a) Causes: leaks from old pipelines and facilities, sabotage and oil theft, accidents, and flaring of associated gas. Effects: polluted creeks and farmland, death of fish and damage to mangroves, loss of livelihoods for farmers and fishermen, air pollution and health problems, and conflict between communities and oil companies.

(b) Regular maintenance and replacement of pipelines; prompt clean-up of spills and compensation for communities; strict enforcement of environmental laws and reduction of gas flaring by using the gas for power or export.
points: (a) Up to 6 marks; (b) 2 marks per measure.

structured.q: (a) Name three tourist attractions in Nigeria and the state where each is found. (b) Describe three problems facing tourism in Nigeria and suggest a solution to each.
model: (a) For example: Obudu Mountain Resort (Cross River); Yankari Game Reserve (Bauchi); Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove (Osun); Argungu Fishing Festival (Kebbi); Olumo Rock (Ogun).

(b) 1. Insecurity in some regions: improve security and community policing around sites. 2. Poor roads and facilities: invest in access roads, power, water and accommodation. 3. Weak maintenance and publicity: train staff, maintain sites and promote them at home and abroad.
points: 1 mark for each attraction and its state (up to 4 marks).
1 mark for each problem and 1 for a matching solution (6 marks).
